Acknowledgments are extended to Marla Sheffer for editing the complete text of the Guidelines, as well as to Windy Prohom and Colette Desigaud for their assistance in project administration. Special thanks are also given to Peter Gosling, who served as the rapporteur for the Final Review Meeting for the finalization of the third edition of the WHO Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater, Excreta, and Greywater in Geneva. The preparation of these Guidelines was made possible through the generous support of the United Kingdom Department for International Development, the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida) via the Stockholm Environment Institute, the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Technische Zusammenarbeit (GTZ), and the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs (DGIS) through WASTE (advisors on urban environment and development). The ultimate goal of these Guidelines is to safeguard and promote public health. At the national level, adequate capacity is required to maximize the benefits of using wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture, while minimizing associated health risks and promoting proper environmental management to ensure long-term sustainability. A critical component of this national capacity is the establishment of an enabling policy environment. This chapter outlines the information necessary to formulate decision-making criteria, establish decision-making procedures, and create effective institutional arrangements for implementation. Good governance necessitates consistency in decision-making to achieve agreed objectives. Policies provide the framework for setting national development priorities and offer decision-making criteria to guide the development process toward achieving these priorities. Policies may lead to the creation of legislation, which defines the responsibilities and rights of various stakeholders. Supported by institutional arrangements between agencies, this determines which agency has the lead responsibility for creating regulations and who has the authority to implement and enforce them. Translating policy into strategy requires the allocation of human and financial resources in alignment with policy objectives and stakeholder capacities. In developing a national policy framework to facilitate the safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture, it is essential to define the objectives of the policies, assess the current policy environment, formulate new policies or adjust existing ones, and develop a national strategy. The use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater can serve multiple objectives. Defining these objectives is the first step in developing a national policy framework. Assessing the existing or potential magnitude of wastewater, excreta, and greywater use, both in absolute and relative terms for different types of use, is key to determining the type of policy formulation or adjustment required. Environmental protection is a policy goal in most countries, focusing on conserving natural resources and ecosystem services while protecting public health. A sectoral view of wastewater, excreta, and greywater often considers them costly by-products of urbanization, requiring substantial investments in treatment plants and disposal mechanisms. However, this perspective overlooks their value as sources of water and nutrients for plant production and fish cultivation. For many developing countries, achieving and maintaining food security for the entire population is a key policy goal. To achieve these goals, some countries provide incentives for increased use of available natural resources, including water resources, for local food production. Others may offer subsidies to farmers to maintain a critical human resource base for local agricultural production. Where national resources for food production are under pressure and essential foods must be imported, governments often provide subsidies to ensure that the poor can meet their basic nutritional needs. In this context, the use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater is particularly relevant. In water-stressed situations, wastewater must be considered a valuable water resource and an important positive trade-off in the process of rapid urbanization. Where essential food items must be imported, waste use to enhance local agricultural production can result in significant import substitutions. Given the above, it is crucial to map out the existing policy landscape and periodically update it as a basis for evaluating whether the options and Guidelines for the safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater are being fully considered and whether safe use practices are being promoted to maximize cost-effectiveness. This includes maximizing economic returns without endangering public health or the environment and ensuring that current and future waste use activities comply with all relevant national and local laws and regulations. Depending on local conditions, policies for the use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater may be emphasized within the food security or environmental protection policy framework. Regardless of the emphasis, effective links must be established with the national public health policy framework to ensure their safe use. The main policy issues to investigate include public health, environmental protection, and food security. Public health considerations involve assessing the extent to which waste management is addressed in national public health policies, identifying specific health hazards and risks associated with the use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture, and determining whether there is a national health impact assessment policy. Environmental protection considerations include evaluating the management of wastewater, excreta, and greywater within the existing environmental protection policy framework, assessing current and potential environmental impacts, and exploring options for reuse in agriculture or aquaculture. Food security considerations involve examining the objectives and criteria outlined in national food security policies, determining whether water is a limiting factor in ensuring national food security, and assessing the opportunities for using wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture to address this issue. Policymakers should use updated evidence on health impacts associated with the use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture to develop rational and cost-effective policies that protect public health and maximize the beneficial use of natural resources.
